title: TTFT, Latency Metrics & Parameter Tuning
desc: Define TTFT, TPOT/ITL, and throughput precisely, benchmark a live vLLM endpoint, and use a tuning playbook to pick the right parameters for your latency SLA.
content:
Why "It Works" Isn't Enough

A vLLM server that returns correct tokens can still fail an SLA. Product wants a chat UI that feels instant; finance wants the fewest GPU-hours per request. Both requirements live inside the same three numbers: TTFT, TPOT (also called inter-token latency, ITL), and throughput. This lesson defines them precisely, shows how to measure them against a live endpoint, and gives you a tuning playbook for trading one against the other — closing the loop back to the capacity math from Day 1's back-of-envelope estimation.

🔑
The Three Numbers That Define "Good Enough"
TTFT — how long until the first token appears (prefill-bound). TPOT/ITL — the steady-state delay between tokens once streaming starts (decode-bound). Throughput — total tokens/sec the fleet sustains across all concurrent requests. You cannot maximize all three at once — every serving decision is a trade between them.

Defining the Metrics

End-to-end latency
Latency = TTFT + TPOT × output_tokens
MetricWhat it measuresBound byWho feels it
TTFTRequest submitted → first token returnedPrefill compute, queueing"Is this thing alive?" — perceived responsiveness
TPOT / ITLAverage gap between consecutive output tokensDecode memory bandwidthStreaming smoothness — stutter vs. steady flow
ThroughputTotal tokens/sec (or req/s) across all concurrent usersBatching efficiency, GPU countCost per token, fleet capacity

Per Anyscale's guide to reproducible LLM metrics, every one of these should be reported as a distribution — P50, P90, P95, P99 — never a single average. vLLM's own bench serve tool reports exactly these four metric families: ttft, tpot, itl, e2el.

⚠️
P50 Lies to You
Median latency looks great right up until the moment a burst of long prompts queues behind it. SLAs should be written against P95/P99, not P50 — the tail is where users notice pain and where on-call gets paged. A server that's fast at P50 but has a 4-second P99 will still generate a steady stream of angry tickets.

Prefill vs. Decode — Why TTFT and TPOT Trade Off Differently

Prefill processes the entire prompt in one parallel forward pass — it's compute-bound, and its cost scales with prompt length. Decode generates one token at a time, re-reading the full KV cache and weights from VRAM on every step — it's memory-bandwidth-bound (see Day 1's roofline discussion). This is why continuous batching engines exist: batching many decode steps together amortizes the same weight read across more tokens, raising throughput — but a big batch sitting in the scheduler also means a new request's prefill has to wait, raising TTFT.

TTFT covers prefill — one big parallel compute step over the whole prompt. Once the first token streams out, TPOT/ITL measures the steady gap between each subsequent token — bound by how fast weights and KV cache can be re-read from VRAM.

Benchmarking a Live Endpoint

vLLM ships a benchmarking client purpose-built for this. Point it at the OpenAI-compatible server you stood up in Day 3:

Shell · vllm bench serve
# Requires: pip install vllm (bench CLI ships with it)
vllm bench serve \
    --backend openai-chat \
    --base-url http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:8000 \
    --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
    --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \
    --dataset-name random \
    --random-input-len 512 \
    --random-output-len 256 \
    --num-prompts 200 \
    --max-concurrency 32 \
    --metric-percentiles 50,90,95,99

If you'd rather measure it yourself (or benchmark a non-vLLM endpoint), a minimal streaming client does the job — capture the wall-clock time of the first chunk versus the time between every chunk after that:

Python · measuring TTFT and TPOT against a streaming endpoint
import time
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed")

start = time.perf_counter()
first_token_time = None
prev_token_time = None
inter_token_gaps = []

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the causes of WWI in 200 words."}],
    max_tokens=256,
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in stream:
    now = time.perf_counter()
    if not chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        continue
    if first_token_time is None:
        first_token_time = now
        prev_token_time = now
        continue
    inter_token_gaps.append(now - prev_token_time)
    prev_token_time = now

ttft = first_token_time - start
tpot = sum(inter_token_gaps) / len(inter_token_gaps)
print(f"TTFT: {ttft*1000:.0f} ms  |  TPOT: {tpot*1000:.1f} ms/token")
💡
Run It Under Load, Not Alone
A single request measured in isolation tells you almost nothing about production TTFT — it tells you the best case. Always benchmark with --max-concurrency set to your expected sustained load; TTFT degrades sharply as queueing kicks in, per Databricks' benchmarking guidance.

The Tuning Playbook

Every one of vLLM's key parameters (introduced in Day 2) sits on the TTFT ↔ throughput ↔ cost trade-off. There is no globally "correct" setting — only the setting correct for your SLA.

ParameterTurn it up →Turn it down →Tune for
max-num-seqsHigher throughput, more $/GPU-hour valueLower TTFT (less queueing per request)Low TTFT priority: keep low (16–64). Throughput priority: raise (128–512)
gpu-memory-utilizationMore room for KV cache → more concurrent seqsSafety margin, less OOM riskRaise toward 0.90–0.95 once you've profiled peak usage
max-model-lenSupports longer contextsSmaller KV cache per sequence → more concurrency headroomCap at what your product actually needs — don't default to the model max
Batch size (implicit, via scheduler)Higher throughputLower per-request latencyContinuous batching (vLLM default) gets you most of both — but extreme concurrency still queues
tensor-parallel-sizeFits larger models, can lower per-token latencyFewer GPUs tied up per replica → more replicas → more aggregate throughputUse the smallest TP that fits the model; prefer more replicas over bigger TP when both are possible
💬 Chat UI — TTFT priority
  • max-num-seqs: 32–64 (cap queueing)
  • enable-prefix-caching: on (shared system prompt)
  • max-model-len: only as large as the UI needs
  • Prefer more small replicas over one big TP group
📦 Batch summarization — throughput priority
  • max-num-seqs: 256+ (let the queue build)
  • gpu-memory-utilization: 0.92–0.95
  • Accept higher per-request TTFT — nobody's watching a spinner
  • Larger TP acceptable if it raises tokens/sec per dollar

Worked Example — Sizing to an SLA

Say product hands you: P99 TTFT < 500 ms, sustained 50 req/s, avg 300 output tokens/request, Llama-3 8B on H100. Chain Day 1's formulas to this lesson's metrics:

  1. KV cache per request (Day 1's kv_cache_bytes formula for Llama-3 8B — 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, fp16 — gives 0.131 MB/token, not a round number, so always derive it from the formula rather than guessing): at a ~2,048-token context (prompt + output), that's 0.131 MB/token × 2048 ≈ 0.27 GB per sequence.
  2. Concurrency needed (Little's Law, Day 1): L = λ × W. With arrival rate λ = 50 req/s and a target average residency W ≈ 2s (TTFT + full decode for 300 tokens at a healthy TPOT), you need roughly L ≈ 100 concurrent in-flight sequences.
  3. VRAM budget for KV cache: 100 sequences × 0.27 GB ≈ 27 GB of KV cache, plus ~16 GB of BF16 weights ≈ 43 GB total — comfortably inside a single 80 GB H100 even after leaving room for activations and CUDA graph buffers. Unlike a 70B-class model (Day 1), memory is not the constraint here — a single GPU can physically hold all 100 sequences.
  4. Conclusion: the limiter is TTFT under queueing, not VRAM. Don't set max-num-seqs to 100+ just because the memory fits — a high value packs more decode work into each scheduler step and makes new arrivals wait longer for their prefill slot. Start with max-num-seqs around 64 on a single replica, measure P99 TTFT with vllm bench serve --max-concurrency 50, and only add a second replica (for redundancy and extra burst headroom, not because you ran out of memory) if that measurement misses the 500 ms target.
📐
The Pattern
Capacity planning (Day 1) tells you how many sequences you can fit. This lesson's metrics tell you whether that many sequences still hits your latency SLA. You need both — a deployment that fits in VRAM but blows through P99 TTFT is just as broken as one that OOMs.
🧠 Check your understanding
1. A team doubles max-num-seqs to raise throughput and finds P99 TTFT gets worse under the same load. Why?
2. Which phase does TPOT (time per output token) primarily measure the cost of?
3. Why should an SLA be written against P99 latency instead of P50 (median)?
4. For a chat product where users watch tokens stream in, which parameter change most directly protects TTFT under bursty traffic?
🔑
Key Takeaways — and the Course, Closed
1. TTFT (prefill) and TPOT/ITL (decode) are different bottlenecks with different fixes — don't tune one when the other is the problem. 2. Report every metric as P95/P99, never an average. 3. Every serving parameter trades TTFT against throughput against cost — pick the point on that curve your SLA actually needs. 4. This whole course is one pipeline: Day 1 sizes the box, Day 2–3 pick and run the engine, Day 4 improves the weights, Day 5 keeps it honest in production, and Day 6 proves it's fast enough — capacity math and latency math are the same spreadsheet.
